partner_context.their_ambition: The City of Toronto runs the island ferries from the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal — around 18,000 riders a day in season across the Inner Harbour to Centre Island, Hanlan's Point and Ward's Island. With a fleet 50 to 100 years old, the City is procuring an all-electric replacement fleet; the ambition is a clean, reliable harbour service for residents and millions of visitors.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the zero-emission, foiling accelerant to a fleet the City is already electrifying. The same Inner Harbour crossings — Jack Layton to Centre Island, Hanlan's Point and Ward's Island — served by fast, near-silent, low-wake foiling ferries that add direct runs and cut crossing times across the harbour.

hero.eyebrow: Authority proposal · City of Toronto, Canada · Toronto Island Ferry
hero.title: Navier × Toronto Island Ferry — the Inner Harbour, on foils
hero.subtitle: A zero-emission foiling layer on the island ferries: faster, direct harbour crossings, cleaner air, and an accelerant to the City's all-electric fleet plan.
hero.what_we_do_together: The City of Toronto brings the island ferry network, the Jack Layton hub and the electrification mandate; Navier brings the foiling-electric fleet, captain training and the certification path. Together we cross the Inner Harbour faster, quieter and zero-emission for 18,000 riders a day.

why_now: Toronto is procuring an all-electric island ferry fleet to replace vessels aged 50–100 years — the ideal moment to add a fast, zero-emission foiling tier that shortens the busiest harbour crossings while the fleet renews.
multimodal_fit: Navier slots into the existing island service — the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal on the mainland at Queens Quay, and the island docks at Centre Island, Hanlan's Point and Ward's Island — taking the high-frequency direct runs while conventional ferries keep heavier seasonal loads. Riders step from streetcar and PATH straight onto a foil across the harbour.

journeys_unlocked.label: Jack Layton ↔ Centre Island
journeys_unlocked.today: The busiest island run is a slow diesel crossing at capacity in summer.
journeys_unlocked.with_navier: The primary island crossing, flown clear of the water — fast, near-silent, zero-emission.

journeys_unlocked.label: Jack Layton ↔ Hanlan's Point
journeys_unlocked.today: The west-island run to Hanlan's Point is a slow seasonal ferry.
journeys_unlocked.with_navier: A quick, clean direct crossing to Hanlan's Point — low-wake and quiet.

journeys_unlocked.label: Jack Layton ↔ Ward's Island
journeys_unlocked.today: The east-island run to Ward's Island residents means the diesel ferry schedule.
journeys_unlocked.with_navier: A fast, zero-emission link to Ward's Island across the Inner Harbour.

differentiation.why_navier: Proven in service and purpose-built for this job: 10x more efficient than a planing hull, low-wake (gentle on a busy recreational harbour), near-silent and zero-emission. It accelerates the City's electrification mandate and adds fast direct crossings across the Inner Harbour.

proof_points.claim: The island ferry is a live municipal service.
proof_points.evidence: The City of Toronto runs year-round service from the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal to Centre Island, Hanlan's Point and Ward's Island — about 18,000 riders a day in peak season.

proof_points.claim: The City is already electrifying the fleet.
proof_points.evidence: Toronto is procuring an all-electric island ferry fleet to replace vessels aged 50–100 years.

proof_points.claim: The platform is proven in service.
proof_points.evidence: 10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out.

objections.concern: Can a foiling ferry work in the Inner Harbour?
objections.response: Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal at the existing docks, flies above the harbour chop for a smoother ride, and its low wake is gentle on a busy recreational harbour and its shoreline.

objections.concern: Is this affordable for a municipal service?
objections.response: Foiling-electric is ~10x more efficient than a diesel planing hull, so fuel — the largest operating cost — falls sharply, complementing the electrification the City is already funding.

objections.concern: Does this replace the ferries people rely on?
objections.response: No — it's a faster layer above them. Conventional ferries keep the heavier seasonal loads; the foiling fleet adds fast, clean direct runs.

the_ask.navier_brings: The software-defined foiling-electric fleet, captain training, and the maintenance and certification path, aligned to Transport Canada requirements.
the_ask.partner_brings: The island ferry network, the Jack Layton hub, and the all-electric fleet-procurement plan.
the_ask.next_step: Pick the first island crossing — most likely Jack Layton–Centre Island — for a zero-emission foiling pilot alongside the fleet procurement.

close.body: The island ferries are how Toronto reaches its harbour every day, and the City is already electrifying them. Navier is how those crossings get faster and cleaner now — a quiet, zero-emission ride across the Inner Harbour for residents and millions of visitors.

end_state.headline: A zero-emission foiling layer across the Toronto Inner Harbour crossings.
end_state.addressable_footprint: The island ferry network — Jack Layton Terminal to Centre Island, Hanlan's Point and Ward's Island — re-platformed onto foiling-electric vessels.

steady_state.total_corridors: Jack Layton to Centre Island, Hanlan's Point and Ward's Island
steady_state.the_opportunity: A fast, zero-emission harbour service for one of North America's great waterfront cities.

end_state.narrative: Steady state is a decarbonised Inner Harbour: the island crossings served by fast, near-silent, low-wake foiling ferries — an accelerant to the City's all-electric fleet.
